title: Eventual linear growth of order under one-coordinate weighting
statement:
Let $F$ be a field, $n\ge1$, $R=F[[u_1,\ldots,u_n]]$ and $S=F[[u_1,\ldots,u_n,t]]$ [def-weil-pbc-multivariate-power-series]. Let $K\subseteq R$ be a nonzero finitely generated ideal. Define $\operatorname{ord}_{(u)}K=\sup\{q:K\subseteq(u_1,\ldots,u_n)^q\}$, and put $a=\max\{v:K\subseteq(u_1)^v\}$. Then $a$ is finite, $K=u_1^aL$ for a nonzero ideal $L$ not contained in $(u_1)$, and the image $\overline L\subset F[[u_2,\ldots,u_n]]$ is nonzero. Put $h=\operatorname{ord}_{(u_2,\ldots,u_n)}\overline L$; when $n=1$ the latter ring is $F$ and $h=0$. For every $k\ge0$ let $K^{[k]}\subseteq S$ be generated by $f(t^ku_1,u_2,\ldots,u_n)$ for a finite generating set of $K$. This definition is independent of the generating set, $K^{[k]}$ is nonzero, and
$$\operatorname{ord}_{(u,t)}K^{[k]}\ge\operatorname{ord}_{(u)}K\quad(k\ge0),\qquad\operatorname{ord}_{(u,t)}K^{[k]}=(k+1)a+h\quad(k\ge h).$$
Consequently $\operatorname{ord}K^{[k+1]}-\operatorname{ord}K^{[k]}=a$ for all $k\ge h$. Here all orders of the nonzero ideals in these formulas are finite. Substitution sends the zero ideal to zero as well, with order $\infty$.

proof.text: Apply [lem-weil-pbc-power-series-combined-ideal-coefficients] with coefficient ring $F$, base ideal $J=0$, and any finite number of variables. It says that $f\in(x)^q$ exactly when every coefficient of total degree less than $q$ is zero. Consequently, for a nonzero ideal generated by finitely many series, its order is the least total degree of a nonzero coefficient occurring among those generators: containment in $(x)^q$ is equivalent to containment of each generator. The least degree exists by well-ordering of $\mathbf N$. This also applies with no variables, where the only exponent is the empty exponent of degree zero.

proof.text:
Choose generators $f_1,\ldots,f_s$ of $K$ and write $u'=(u_2,\ldots,u_n)$. By the coefficient definition [def-weil-pbc-multivariate-power-series], a series $\sum c_{e, eta}u_1^e(u')^ eta$ is divisible by $u_1^v$ if and only if its coefficients with $e<v$ vanish: the quotient has coefficients $c_{v+e, eta}$. Let $a$ be the least first exponent among nonzero coefficients of the $f_j$. This set is nonempty since $K
e0$. Thus $K\subseteq(u_1)^a$ and some generator is not in $(u_1)^{a+1}$, proving the asserted maximum is finite. Put $f_j=u_1^ag_j$ and $L=(g_1,\ldots,g_s)$. Then $K=u_1^aL$, and some $g_j$ has a nonzero coefficient with first exponent zero. Hence $L
ot\subseteq(u_1)$ and $\overline L=(g_j(0,u'))
e0$. This $L$ is the only ideal with $K=u_1^aL$: multiplication by $u_1^a$ shifts coefficients, so it is injective, and any such ideal equals $\{x:u_1^ax\in K\}$. Hence $\overline L$ and $h$ depend only on $K$.

proof.text: Define $\sigma_k:R\to S$ on coefficients by sending the term $c_{e,\beta}u_1^e(u')^\beta$ to $c_{e,\beta}t^{ke}u_1^e(u')^\beta$. The exponent map $(e,\beta)\mapsto(e,\beta,ke)$ is injective and additive. Therefore this formula defines a coefficient family, preserves sums and constants, and preserves products: the finite Cauchy sum at an image exponent is precisely the sum over the decompositions of $(e,\beta)$, while at a non-image exponent every summand is zero. It follows directly from [def-weil-pbc-multivariate-power-series] that $\sigma_k$ is an injective $F$-algebra homomorphism, including $k=0$. This constructs the substitution in the statement without any convergence assumption.

proof.text: If $f=\sum_j b_jf_j$ is in $K$, the homomorphism identity gives $\sigma_k(f)=\sum_j\sigma_k(b_j)\sigma_k(f_j)$. Thus the ideal generated by the $\sigma_k(f_j)$ equals the ideal generated by all $\sigma_k(f)$ with $f\in K$, and is independent of the generating set. It is nonzero by injectivity. Moreover, with $L^{[k]}=(\sigma_k(g_j))$, the identity $\sigma_k(u_1^ag_j)=t^{ka}u_1^a\sigma_k(g_j)$ gives $K^{[k]}=t^{ka}u_1^aL^{[k]}$. Multiplication by this monomial shifts every nonzero coefficient's total degree by $(k+1)a$, without changing its value.

proof.text: Each nonzero coefficient of $f_j$ at $(e,\beta)$ becomes a nonzero coefficient of $\sigma_k(f_j)$ of total degree $(k+1)e+|\beta|\ge e+|\beta|$. Applying the coefficient criterion [lem-weil-pbc-power-series-combined-ideal-coefficients] to the finite lists in $R$ and $S$, as in step 1, proves $\operatorname{ord}_{(u,t)}K^{[k]}\ge\operatorname{ord}_{(u)}K$ for every $k\ge0$. The orders are finite because both lists contain a nonzero series.

proof.text: Apply step 1 to the nonzero ideal $\overline L$ generated by $g_j(0,u')$. Its finite order $h$ is the least $|\beta|$ of a nonzero coefficient of some $g_j$ with first exponent zero, and this least degree is attained. If $n=1$, the empty exponent gives $h=0$. For $k\ge h$, every term with first exponent zero in $\sigma_k(g_j)$ has degree at least $h$, and one has degree exactly $h$. Every term with first exponent $e\ge1$ has degree $(k+1)e+|\beta|\ge k+1>h$. Distinct source exponents remain distinct, so the degree-$h$ witness survives. The coefficient criterion [lem-weil-pbc-power-series-combined-ideal-coefficients] now gives $\operatorname{ord}L^{[k]}=h$. The monomial shift in step 4 therefore gives $\operatorname{ord}K^{[k]}=(k+1)a+h$.

proof.text: For $k\ge h$, the formula applies to both $k$ and $k+1$; subtracting gives $((k+2)a+h)-((k+1)a+h)=a$. All these quantities are finite by steps 1, 5 and 6, so no subtraction involving infinity occurs. Finally $\sigma_k(0)=0$, and the ideal generated by zero is zero. It is contained in every power of the variables ideal and thus has order $\infty$, as stipulated.
